h3.h3: The tool categories an audit has to cover: resume screening, matching, video interviews, assessments

evidence.gloss: Automated resume screening uses NLP/ML to rank candidates fast and reduce bias versus manual review.
evidence.verbatim:
An average job posting receives 500 applications; reviewing each resume is time-consuming for recruiters.
Automated resume screening tools use natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) to review thousands of resumes in a fraction of the time it would take a human recruiter to do so.
These tools can identify keywords, relevant experiences, and qualifications, ranking candidates based on how well their resumes match job descriptions. This accelerates the initial screening process and helps reduce human bias by focusing on data-driven criteria.

evidence.gloss: AI algorithms match candidate profiles to job requirements more accurately than manual screening.
evidence.verbatim: AI-driven tools use sophisticated algorithms to analyze candidate profiles and compare them against job requirements. This ensures more accurate and efficient candidate matching, increasing the likelihood of finding the best-fit candidates for open positions. The result is a more targeted and streamlined hiring process.

evidence.gloss: AI-based video/audio interview platforms analyze responses and tone; Testlify's interview tool cuts hiring time.
evidence.verbatim:
AI-based interview platforms are changing the way organizations conduct initial candidate interviews. Using video interviews and AI analytics, these tools assess candidates’ responses, body language, and vocal tones to gauge their suitability for a role.
This technology allows recruiters to focus on the most promising candidates while automating parts of the interview process.
Testlify offers video and audio interviews, which enable employers to assess candidates’ communication skills and cultural fit more dynamically and engagingly, providing valuable insights beyond what traditional interviews can capture.
Recruiters can use audio questions to check candidate’s verbal communication, critical thinking, problem-solving, etc. This is especially useful when assessing specific skills or abilities required for a particular role.
Check out how you can slash hiring time by 90% using Testlify’s video interviewing tool.

evidence.gloss: AI-driven pre-employment assessments improve hire quality over resumes/cover letters; Testlify's 1500+ test library example.
evidence.verbatim:
AI-driven pre-employment assessments transform candidate evaluation. 78% of recruiters say AI assessments have improved the quality of their hires. HR professionals no longer need to rely on traditional sources like resumes or cover letters, which 58% of candidates admit to manipulating.
As hiring managers increasingly prioritize soft skills, pre-employment assessments comprehensively assess a candidate’s skill set, knowledge, and competencies. Testlify provides an extensive library of 1500+ tests customized for 50+ roles.
These assessments provide objective insights into candidates’ abilities, minimize unconscious bias, and help employers make informed hiring decisions.

h3.h3: Keyword-based resume scanning filters out qualified candidates

evidence.gloss: Keyword-based resume scanning can filter out qualified candidates who don't use the exact terms the algorithm searches for; suggests skills assessments as an alternative.
evidence.verbatim: AI often scans resumes for particular keywords. This will disadvantage some applicants who may have the needed skills but do not use the terms the algorithm searches for. Such reliance on keywords can easily lead to the absence of viable candidates. Using skills assessments in place of screening resumes helps shortlist the right candidates for the role.

sections_menu.h2: The parts of an AI recruitment stack and where bias enters

h3.h3: Parsing, screening, assessment, and chat are separate systems

evidence.gloss: Parsing, screening, assessments, and conversational AI are functionally distinct despite being bundled
evidence.verbatim: Resume parsing, screening, assessments, and conversational AI get sold as one bundle but are functionally distinct: parsing extracts data into fields and is data cleanup, not a decision; screening applies criteria to decide who advances; assessments measure skills or job simulations as inputs into screening; and conversational AI runs a chat or SMS flow to capture availability.[11]

evidence.gloss: ML is a small fraction of build effort
evidence.verbatim: Practitioners who build these pipelines report that the model itself is a small fraction of the work — machine learning accounts for roughly a fifth of the build, with the rest going to data hygiene, threshold policy, and audit plumbing.[10]

evidence.gloss: Parse-confidence scoring routes low-confidence docs to human queue
evidence.verbatim: PDFs from design tools, two-column layouts, and scanned documents degrade parse quality, so a defensible system logs a parse-confidence score per document and routes anything under threshold to a human queue rather than letting a document that failed to parse score badly and disappear.[10]

h3.h3: Knockout criteria and the years-of-experience problem

evidence.gloss: Knockout criteria are hard legally-defensible facts
evidence.verbatim: Knockout criteria come next: hard, legally defensible facts such as right to work, a required license, a security clearance, or minimum shift availability.

evidence.gloss: Years-of-experience cutoffs are the most contested knockout criterion
evidence.verbatim: These are supposed to be deterministic rules, not a model, and years-of-experience cutoffs are the criterion vendors most often hard-code and the one that draws the most pushback, because it correlates with age and predicts performance poorly.[10]

h3.h3: Name bias in resume screening, and anonymization as a response

evidence.gloss: UW study: LLMs favor white-associated resume names far more than Black-associated names
evidence.verbatim: A University of Washington study of more than 3 million resume comparisons found large language models preferred white-associated names 85% of the time versus just 9% for Black-associated names (UW, 2024), illustrating how algorithmic selection can inherit and concentrate historical bias rather than dilute it[12].

evidence.gloss: This study is the empirical basis for treating adverse-impact testing as mandatory for AI tools
evidence.verbatim: This is the empirical basis for treating adverse-impact testing as a necessary check on any AI-driven selection tool, not an optional add-on for traditional human-scored assessments.

evidence.gloss: Unilever anonymizes resumes with AI during initial screening to cut unconscious bias and boost diversity.
evidence.verbatim: Unilever has embraced AI to address diversity and inclusion challenges. By using AI tools to anonymize resumes during the initial screening process, Unilever aims to reduce unconscious bias and ensure that candidates are evaluated based on their skills and qualifications.

sections_menu.h2: Where bias enters an AI recruitment tool

h3.h3: The failure modes: data bias, measurement bias, and the five points a screening pipeline breaks

evidence.gloss: Bias arises from multiple distinct failure modes, not one defect
evidence.verbatim: Bias in AI hiring systems is described as arising from multiple, distinct failure modes rather than a single defect[6][8]:

evidence.gloss: Data bias defined
evidence.verbatim: **data bias** (training data reflecting historical inequities — résumé corpora underrepresenting women in engineering, interview transcripts over-indexing on one accent)[6];

evidence.gloss: Measurement bias defined
evidence.verbatim: **measurement bias** (optimizing for proxies that don't match the actual construct being hired for)[6];

evidence.gloss: Other bias sources across the recruitment pipeline
evidence.verbatim: and biases introduced through label definitions, feature selection, proxies, and masking across the recruitment pipeline[8].

evidence.gloss: Screening pipeline has five discrete audit-failure points
evidence.verbatim: A resume screening pipeline runs through five discrete stages, and each one is a separate point where an audit can fail the tool.[10]

evidence.gloss: Bias mechanism consistently traces to training data
evidence.verbatim: The mechanism behind these outcomes is consistent across cases: bias traces to the training data.

evidence.gloss: Tools reproduce past hiring bias and pick up proxies for protected traits
evidence.verbatim: When a tool learns from past hiring decisions that favored one group, it reproduces that preference in screening or scoring, and it can also pick up proxies for protected traits, such as a zip code that correlates with race, without a protected attribute ever appearing as a model input.[14][15]

evidence.gloss: Covers trust and fairness risks, including algorithmic bias from historical hiring data and accent-based scoring issues.
evidence.verbatim:
The trust gap is real. Candidates are increasingly skeptical of algorithms that reject them without explanation.
If an AI is trained on historical hiring data where only certain demographics were hired, it can repeat those patterns. This is how bias can show up. Some research suggests that some LLMs score candidates lower based on regional accents or cultural expressions, even if they are highly qualified.

h3.h3: Bias at the sourcing stage: Pin and the pool-construction approach

evidence.gloss: Pin addresses bias at the sourcing stage rather than the scoring stage
evidence.verbatim: Pin is cited as an example of a tool addressing bias at the sourcing stage rather than the scoring stage.

evidence.gloss: Narrow sourcing channels cap downstream selection rate and narrow the demographic mix pre-screening
evidence.verbatim: Because the applicant pool caps every downstream selection rate, sourcing from a single network, university list, or referral chain narrows the demographic mix before screening even begins

evidence.gloss: Pin pulls candidates from multiple channels (professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, patents, academic publications) to widen the pool
evidence.verbatim: Pin instead pulls candidates from multiple channels — professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, patents, and academic publications — as a multi-source approach intended to widen the starting pool[12]

evidence.gloss: No bias-audit or disclosure evidence exists for Pin; evidence is about pool-construction method only
evidence.verbatim: No bias-audit result, adverse-impact ratio, or Local Law 144 disclosure is cited for Pin specifically; the evidence here is about pool-construction methodology rather than a tested outcome.

evidence.gloss: Best practices for diversity: anonymous screening, bias-free job description checks, and inclusive sourcing to reach underrepresented candidates.
evidence.verbatim:
- Anonymous screening: Using AI to remove personal details like name, gender, and age from resumes can help reduce bias during the initial screening process.
- Bias-free job descriptions: AI tools can analyze job descriptions to ensure they don’t contain biased language that might deter certain candidates from applying.
- Inclusive sourcing: AI can be used to identify and reach out to candidates from underrepresented groups, helping to widen the talent pool.

h3.h3: What actually contains it: regular audits, explainable scoring, and human oversight

evidence.gloss: AI bias risk from training data, with Testlify's bias-monitoring and fairness-focused assessment design as mitigation.
evidence.verbatim:
Research shows that 49% of respondents believe AI in hiring introduces more bias than human decision-making.
AI systems are often trained on historical pre-programmed data, which can have inherent biases. If left unchecked, such bias might amplify and lead to unfair hiring decisions, eventually impacting diversity in the workplace.
Testlify’s AI-powered assessments are designed with diversity and fairness in mind. The platform continually monitors and evaluates its algorithms to identify potential biases and take corrective action.
Additionally, Testlify’s AI assessments focus on objective skills and job-relevant criteria, reducing the reliance on subjective factors that could lead to biased outcomes.

evidence.gloss: Recommends regular bias audits, diverse training data, and human oversight as ways recruiters can counter AI bias.
evidence.verbatim:
- Regular audits: AI systems should be regularly audited for bias. This includes looking at the data that the AI is being trained on, as well as how it evaluates candidates over time.
- Diverse data: The data sets that train AI should be diverse and inclusive, representing a broad spectrum of candidates.
- Human oversight: AI should not be the final decision-maker. Human oversight is crucial to ensure fairness and catch any red flags the AI might miss.

evidence.gloss: Recommends choosing AI vendors focused on ethical, bias-restricted, regularly audited systems.
evidence.verbatim: Use vendors that focus on ethical AI. This means that the same AI systems are built to restrict bias and are monitored through regular audits in those systems, in which audit challenges them further to ensure the system’s equity.

evidence.gloss: Step 3: choose explainable AI tools that can justify candidate rankings with clear, job-related reasons.
evidence.verbatim:
In 2026, black-box hiring is a bad idea. If a tool ranks candidates, you should be able to explain why. Not with vague promises, but with clear signals: what criteria it used, what it ignored, and whether there’s an audit trail for decisions.
During vendor evaluation, a simple test works well: ask the tool to justify why Candidate A is ranked above Candidate B. If it can’t give a clear, job-related reason, you’ll struggle to trust it internally and you’ll struggle to defend it externally.

sections_menu.h2: The measured evidence on bias in AI recruitment tools

h3.h3: Audit and benchmark results across vendors

evidence.gloss: Warden AI dataset description and 85% four-fifths pass rate
evidence.verbatim: Warden AI's dataset, described as drawn from 150+ bias audits of production AI systems in live hiring workflows, reports: 85% of audited AI hiring systems scored above the 0.8 impact ratio threshold across all tested demographic groups (the EEOC four-fifths bar),

evidence.gloss: 95% counterfactual consistency stat from Warden AI dataset
evidence.verbatim: 95% scored above 97.5% on counterfactual consistency, meaning outputs stayed stable when protected attributes were swapped in otherwise identical profiles[4].

evidence.gloss: Bias varies up to 40% between vendors
evidence.verbatim: That aggregate picture is not uniform across vendors: bias varies by up to 40% between vendors, with some systems clustering near 1.0 (near-perfect parity) and others falling below the four-fifths threshold for at least one protected group[4].

evidence.gloss: 15% of tools failed a demographic threshold, linked to historical training data
evidence.verbatim: In the same 2025 dataset, 15% of audited AI tools failed at least one demographic threshold, and these failures clustered in tools trained primarily on historical hiring data — i.e., on outputs of the human bias AI was meant to correct[4].

evidence.gloss: FAIRE Benchmark found racial/gender disparities in LLM screeners
evidence.verbatim: A separate, standardized test, the FAIRE Benchmark (2025), found significant racial and gender disparities in candidate scoring across LLM-based screeners[6].

h3.h3: Documented bias findings in real screening tools

evidence.gloss: 2021 Harvard study: automated screening rejected 27M+ workers
evidence.verbatim: A 2021 Harvard Business School study found that automated resume screening systems rejected more than 27 million workers.[12]

evidence.gloss: UW study found White-associated names preferred 85% of the time
evidence.verbatim: A University of Washington Information School study by researchers Kyra Wilson and Aylin Caliskan, presented at the October AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, audited three popular open-source large language models used for resume screening and found that resumes carrying White-associated names were preferred 85% of the time over identical resumes with names associated with other demographics.[13]

evidence.gloss: A screening tool was withdrawn for scoring women's resumes lower
evidence.verbatim: A separate case, referenced in a survey of AI fairness research, describes a resume-screening tool that was withdrawn after it was found to systematically assign lower scores to resumes from women, traced back to their underrepresentation in the tool's training data.[14]

evidence.gloss: Stanford Oct 2025 finding: bias toward older male candidates
evidence.verbatim: In October 2025, Stanford researchers found that AI resume-screening tools gave older male candidates higher ratings than both female candidates and younger candidates, even when all resumes were generated from the same underlying data.[27]

evidence.gloss: VoxDev May 2025 finding: bias favoring female over Black male applicants
evidence.verbatim: Research published through VoxDev in May 2025 found that AI hiring tools systematically favored female applicants over Black male applicants with otherwise identical qualifications.[27]

h3.h3: The baseline: how widely these tools are used, and how human bias compares

evidence.gloss: 2022 survey on prevalence of tech-driven job interviews
evidence.verbatim: A 2022 survey found up to 86% of employers reported using technology-driven job interviews, with automated video interviews a common method — indicating the scale of exposure these audit standards are meant to govern[8].

evidence.gloss: EEOC baseline: most discrimination claims are human-driven, not AI
evidence.verbatim: These findings sit against a broader baseline: EEOC enforcement and litigation statistics show that more than 99.9% of employment discrimination claims filed in the U.S. over the last five years relate to human decision-making rather than AI, out of roughly 100,000 claims filed annually and about 100 that progress to lawsuits — only a small fraction of which involve algorithmic systems.[4]

sections_menu.h2: The legal framework a bias audit measures against

h3.h3: Adverse impact, disparate impact, and disparate treatment under Title VII and the UGESP

evidence.gloss: Adverse impact, disparate impact, and disparate treatment are distinct concepts
evidence.verbatim: Adverse impact (the statistical evidence) is distinct from disparate impact (the legal theory it triggers) and disparate treatment (the intentional-discrimination theory)[12].

evidence.gloss: Title VII's two liability theories, rooted in Griggs v. Duke Power and the 1991 Civil Rights Act
evidence.verbatim: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 recognizes disparate treatment and disparate impact as separate liability theories; the Supreme Court established disparate impact liability in Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (1971), and Congress codified it in the Civil Rights Act of 1991[12].

evidence.gloss: UGESP's regulatory definition of adverse impact
evidence.verbatim: UGESP itself defines adverse impact as a selection rate that "works to the disadvantage of members of a race, sex or ethnic group" (29 CFR § 1607.4(D), 1978)[12].

h3.h3: How the EEOC applies that framework to AI hiring tools, and who carries the liability

evidence.gloss: EEOC's May 2023 technical assistance document applies the framework to AI hiring tools
evidence.verbatim: On May 18, 2023, the EEOC issued a technical assistance document, "Assessing Adverse Impact in Software, Algorithms, and Artificial Intelligence Used in Employment Selection Procedures Under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964," applying the disparate-impact framework directly to algorithmic hiring tools and the four-fifths rule as its rule of thumb[18].

evidence.gloss: Employers, not AI vendors, bear liability for discriminatory tool outcomes
evidence.verbatim: That guidance holds employers — not vendors — liable for discriminatory outcomes from third-party AI hiring products; a licensed tool's bias does not transfer liability to the vendor[18].

evidence.gloss: Cites rising EEOC bias investigations and argues companies must document fairness and bias testing to reduce legal risk.
evidence.verbatim:
Forbes reported that the EEOC opened 23% more bias-related hiring investigations year over year. Therefore, companies operating in Europe must document fairness, bias testing, and human oversight for every AI-driven assessment.
The takeaway is clear: Companies that invest in fair assessments today build compliant hiring systems that reduce legal risk and strengthen employer brand.

h3.h3: The April 2025 enforcement shift, and why the exposure has not gone away

evidence.gloss: April 2025 executive order pushed EEOC to deprioritize disparate-impact enforcement
evidence.verbatim: An April 2025 federal executive order directed the EEOC to deprioritize disparate-impact-only enforcement, and the EEOC has moved to stop investigating charges based on disparate impact alone[12][10].

evidence.gloss: Legal exposure persists: Title VII unchanged, private plaintiffs retain standing
evidence.verbatim: the underlying Title VII law has not changed and private plaintiffs retain full standing to sue regardless of federal enforcement priorities[12][10]

evidence.gloss: Legal exposure persists: state/local AEDT laws (NYC Local Law 144, CA/IL/CO) still apply
evidence.verbatim: state and local requirements continue independently — New York City's AEDT bias-audit law (Local Law 144) references the four-fifths rule directly, and California, Illinois, and Colorado have introduced AI/anti-discrimination requirements built on the same principle[12][10]

evidence.gloss: Legal exposure persists: 80% threshold remains the practical cross-jurisdiction benchmark
evidence.verbatim: the 80% threshold remains a practical, widely-used benchmark for employers operating across multiple jurisdictions[10]

h3.h3: State, local, and cross-border AEDT rules: disclosure duties and ongoing assessments

evidence.gloss: Jurisdictions requiring disclosure of AI evaluation to candidates
evidence.verbatim: Illinois, the EU AI Act, and Ontario all require disclosure to candidates that they are being evaluated by an AI interview tool[7].

evidence.gloss: Colorado AI Act (Feb 2026) requires ongoing impact assessments, not one-time validation
evidence.verbatim: Elsewhere, regulators are moving from annual snapshots toward continuous obligation: the Colorado AI Act, effective February 2026, explicitly requires ongoing impact assessments rather than a single pre-deployment validation.[21]

evidence.gloss: Covers legal and compliance obligations for AI hiring tools, citing NYC Local Law 144 and the EU AI Act's high-risk classification.
evidence.verbatim:
If your AI tool is used to screen, rank, recommend, or make decisions, you may be expected to show how it works, how you assessed risk, and what you did to reduce bias.
- In New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Local Law 144 requires employers using automated employment decision tools to have an independent bias audit, publish a summary, and provide notices.
- Under the European Union AI Act framework, AI used in employment-related contexts is treated as high-risk in the Act’s high-risk use-case list, which comes with additional obligations.

sections_menu.h2: NYC Local Law 144: which hiring tools it covers and what it requires

h3.h3: The law itself: dates, obligations, and who falls under it

evidence.gloss: Local Law 144 enactment and purpose
evidence.verbatim: New York City Local Law 144, enacted 11 December 2021, targets discrimination caused by automated employment decision tools (AEDTs) and holds employers and employment agencies accountable for outcomes those tools produce[1].

evidence.gloss: Effective date pushed back three times to enforcement date
evidence.verbatim: The law took effect 1 January 2023, but after two rounds of public comment (a hearing 4 November 2022, revised rules 23 December 2022, a second hearing 23 January 2023), the enforcement date was pushed back three times before settling on 5 July 2023[2][1].

evidence.gloss: Final rules dropped cross-validation requirement
evidence.verbatim: Notably, the final rules dropped the earlier requirement that the technique allow inputs to be refined via cross-validation or training/testing data[2].

evidence.gloss: NYC Local Law 144 requires annual independent third-party bias audit
evidence.verbatim: For a resume screening tool operating on a New York City applicant, NYC Local Law 144 requires an independent bias audit conducted at least once a year, by a third party not involved in developing or using the tool, on a cadence that makes compliance an ongoing commitment rather than a one-time project.[17][18]

evidence.gloss: Local Law 144 doesn't ban AI hiring tools; it conditions AEDT use on three obligations
evidence.verbatim: Local Law 144 does not ban AI in hiring — it makes the use of a covered automated employment decision tool (AEDT) in New York City conditional on three obligations: an independent bias audit conducted within one year before use, public disclosure of a results summary, and specific notice to candidates and employees[1].

evidence.gloss: who the law covers: employers/agencies using an AEDT to hire, promote, or screen
evidence.verbatim: These conditions apply to any employer or employment agency using an AEDT for hiring or promotion, or to screen candidates in that process[2].

evidence.gloss: effective date, final rules release date, and enforcement start date differ
evidence.verbatim: The law took effect January 1, 2023, but the DCWP's final implementing rules were only released April 6, 2023, and enforcement did not begin until July 5, 2023[3].

evidence.gloss: law's geographic trigger is candidate/employee residence, not employer location
evidence.verbatim: Local Law 144 applies based on where the candidate or employee resides, not where the employer is headquartered or where the role is performed[8].

evidence.gloss: out-of-NYC employers are covered if the candidate lives in NYC
evidence.verbatim: An employer does not need to be based in NYC — if a candidate lives in any of the five boroughs, evaluating that candidate with an AEDT triggers the law[4][8].

h3.h3: The AEDT test is functional, not technical

evidence.gloss: Scope of AEDTs covered by the law
evidence.verbatim: Local Law 144 applies to AEDTs used in hiring and recruitment, promotion, and performance evaluation/workforce management, covering any NYC-based position or a remote position connected to NYC[3].

evidence.gloss: Definition of covered ML/AI technique
evidence.verbatim: The final rules define the covered "machine learning, statistical modeling, data analytics, or artificial intelligence" as techniques that (1) generate a prediction (an expected outcome, such as fit or likelihood of success) or a classification (assignment to a group, such as skill-set categorization), and (2) for which a computer at least in part identifies the inputs and their relative importance to improve accuracy[2].

evidence.gloss: Audit required even for early-stage screening use
evidence.verbatim: The rules clarify that a bias audit is required even when the AEDT is only used to "screen" candidates early in the process, not just for the final hiring decision[2].

evidence.gloss: AEDT status turns on function (screen/rank/score), not technical sophistication
evidence.verbatim: The determining question is not the tool's technical sophistication but whether it screens, ranks, or scores

evidence.gloss: A tool is an AEDT if a human treats its output as a significant factor in advancement
evidence.verbatim: if a human reviewer treats the bot's output as a significant factor in who advances, the tool is an AEDT[19][18].

evidence.gloss: Producing a score/ranking/recommendation a recruiter relies on crosses into AEDT territory
evidence.verbatim: The moment that same tool produces a score, ranking, or advance/reject recommendation that a recruiter relies on as a significant factor, it crosses into AEDT territory and the audit, notice, and posting obligations attach[19][29].

evidence.gloss: Qualification test is functional, not technical
evidence.verbatim: The test is not technical sophistication but function: if a tool does more than organize information — if it produces a recommendation, ranking, or score that influences who advances — it likely qualifies[17].

evidence.gloss: Tool types covered by the definition
evidence.verbatim: This covers resume screening, assessment scoring, video-interview analysis, and candidate ranking[18].

h3.h3: Chatbot and conversational screening tools, and the carve-outs

evidence.gloss: Chatbot-based screening defined and classified as an AEDT when it substantially assists or replaces human decisions
evidence.verbatim: Chatbot-based screening — a bot that poses a fixed set of predetermined questions to a candidate, collects the responses within a set timeframe, and evaluates the answers to advance or reject them — falls squarely inside the legal definition of an Automated Employment Decision Tool (AEDT) whenever it "substantially assists or replaces" a human decision-maker in the hiring pipeline[19].

evidence.gloss: NYC Local Law 144 names chatbot assessments alongside other AEDT categories
evidence.verbatim: The NYC Local Law 144 test is explicit on this category: "chatbot assessments that evaluate candidate responses" are named alongside resume-ranking tools, video-interview scoring platforms, and candidate-matching algorithms as tools employers must inventory and audit[19].

evidence.gloss: Academic description of the AI chatbot interviewing mechanism
evidence.verbatim: Academic research on AI-enabled interviewing describes the underlying mechanism: a chatbot poses a set of predetermined questions to the interviewee, gives them a brief window to respond, then collects data on the candidate's visual, verbal, and vocal cues to generate an automated prediction of job suitability (Jaser and Petrakaki, 2023)[31].

evidence.gloss: AI chatbot interviews distinguished from traditional video interviews lacking AI decision-making
evidence.verbatim: This is distinguished from a traditional video interview, which uses telecommunication technology but does not involve any AI decision-making component[31] — a line that maps directly onto the compliance boundary regulators draw.

evidence.gloss: Not every candidate-facing conversational tool triggers an audit obligation
evidence.verbatim: Not every conversational tool touching candidates triggers an audit obligation.

evidence.gloss: Non-scoring tools (translate/transcribe/capture) are carved out of AEDT scope
evidence.verbatim: Tools that "translate, transcribe, or capture data without scoring" are explicitly carved out of AEDT scope[29].

evidence.gloss: Example of a chatbot that is not subject to the bias-audit requirement
evidence.verbatim: A chatbot that only gathers availability, answers FAQs, or logs responses for a human to read later is not itself subject to the bias-audit requirement.

h3.h3: Inventorying your HR tech stack to find covered tools

evidence.gloss: Employers must document per tool what data it ingests and whether it scores or substantially assists a decision
evidence.verbatim: Employers building or buying chatbot screening tools need to document, per tool, what data it ingests (resumes, video, assessment responses), whether it produces a score or classification, and whether that output substantially assists or replaces a human decision[19].

evidence.gloss: Inventory HR tech stack to find AEDT/ADMT-covered systems
evidence.verbatim: Before scheduling anything, inventory the HR technology stack to determine which systems meet the legal definition of an Automated Employment Decision Tool (AEDT) or Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT)[17][18].

evidence.gloss: Inventory framed as foundation of compliance strategy
evidence.verbatim: For large organizations, this internal inventory is described as "the foundation of a clear and defensible compliance strategy"[17].

sections_menu.h2: The data a bias audit runs on

evidence.gloss: Independent auditor qualification requirements
evidence.verbatim: An independent auditor cannot be anyone currently or previously involved in developing, using, or distributing the tool, cannot have an employment relationship with the employer/agency/vendor during the audit, and cannot hold a direct or material indirect financial interest in any of those parties[1].

h3.h3: Historical data versus test data

evidence.gloss: Historical data preferred over test data as audit input
evidence.verbatim: Historical data from real-world use of the tool is the preferred audit input; test data can substitute only if historical data is insufficient or the tool hasn't yet been used, and that substitution must be disclosed[1].

evidence.gloss: Aggregated audit pooling data across employers
evidence.verbatim: Employers can also rely on an aggregated audit that pools historical data across multiple employers using the same tool, provided they contributed data or never used the tool themselves[1].

evidence.gloss: Audit runs on historical use data; test data substitution must be disclosed
evidence.verbatim: The audit must run on historical data from the tool's actual use in employment decisions; if insufficient historical data exists, the auditor may substitute test data but must clearly disclose that substitution in the audit summary.[20]

evidence.gloss: Trade-off between including repeats and filtering them out
evidence.verbatim: Including every instance in the audit dataset risks skewing the sample, but manually filtering instances risks the appearance of cherry-picking the data.[26]

evidence.gloss: Rules on whose historical data an audit may use
evidence.verbatim: On data sourcing, an audit must generally rely on the employer's own historical usage data; a bias audit may use another employer's or agency's historical data only if that other party supplied its own historical AEDT data to the auditor, or if the employer has never used the tool being audited.

evidence.gloss: Test data substitution requires disclosure
evidence.verbatim: Where historical data is insufficient, test data may be substituted, but the published audit summary must explain why historical data wasn't used and describe how the test data was generated and obtained.[2]

evidence.gloss: Demographic and score data split across employer and vendor
evidence.verbatim: Demographic information for a candidate is commonly held only by the employer, while the AEDT's score outputs are held by the vendor, and matching the two data sets for testing requires cooperation across both parties.[26]

evidence.gloss: Historical Data is the default required data source
evidence.verbatim: The audit must rely on Historical Data — the results of the employer's prior use of the specific AEDT — unless the employer can explain why there is insufficient Historical Data available[34][2].

evidence.gloss: Test Data defined as fallback when Historical Data is insufficient
evidence.verbatim: Only with that justification may the audit fall back on Test Data, defined simply as "not Historical Data," meaning independent data sets run through the tool to generate results[34].

evidence.gloss: Rules for borrowing other employers' historical data
evidence.verbatim: If there is insufficient Historical Data containing demographic information — for example, because the employer never collected it — the auditor may use the historical data of other employers or employment agencies, provided that data was contributed to the auditor by an employer that either used the AEDT itself or never used it[2][37].

evidence.gloss: DCWP sets no statistical significance requirement for Test Data
evidence.verbatim: Independent auditors have discretion over when to use Test Data, and the DCWP has explicitly stated it has "not set a specific requirement for statistical significance" and there are "no set requirements for test data," beyond requiring the audit summary to disclose the source and explain how the test data was generated[37].

evidence.gloss: Summary must justify Test Data use and its provenance
evidence.verbatim: Where Test Data is used, the summary must explain why Historical Data was unavailable and describe the test data's provenance[20].

h3.h3: The demographic breakdowns an audit must report

evidence.gloss: NYC's required demographic categories
evidence.verbatim: NYC's required demographic categories for these calculations are sex/gender (male, female, other) and race/ethnicity (Hispanic or Latino, White, Black or African American, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, Asian, Native American or Alaska Native, and two or more races), plus their intersections.[23]

evidence.gloss: AEDT bias audits must report rates/ratios across specific breakdowns
evidence.verbatim: For automated employment decision tools (AEDTs), audits must report selection or scoring rates and impact ratios for[14]:

evidence.gloss: Required breakdown: sex categories
evidence.verbatim: Sex categories

evidence.gloss: Required breakdown: race and ethnicity categories
evidence.verbatim: Race and ethnicity categories (typically following EEOC component groupings)

evidence.gloss: Required breakdown: sex x race/ethnicity intersections
evidence.verbatim: Intersections of sex with race and ethnicity (e.g.

evidence.gloss: Classification-system audits compare to the highest-scoring category; regression scores get binarized at the median
evidence.verbatim: This same intersectional requirement appears in bias-audit methodology for classification systems: the impact ratio compares the selection rate for a category to the selection rate of the highest-scoring category, and for regression systems that output a continuous score, outcomes must first be binarized — individuals are designated pass/fail based on whether their score sits above or below the median score for the audit dataset — before the same ratio calculation applies[15].

evidence.gloss: Ratios required for both standalone and intersectional demographic groups
evidence.verbatim: These ratios must be calculated for both standalone groups (e.g., male, female) and intersectional groups (e.g., Black male, Black female)[15].

h3.h3: Small samples and intersectional testing

evidence.gloss: Small-sample category exclusion rule
evidence.verbatim: Auditors may exclude a race/ethnicity or sex category representing a small sample (a category under 2% of the audit data can be excluded from the analysis, though its scoring/selection rate must still be calculated)[1].

evidence.gloss: EEOC recommends 1,000+ applicants per protected class for statistical power
evidence.verbatim: The EEOC's 2023 Technical Assistance Document recommends testing on a sample of at least 1,000 applicants per protected class to reach statistical power sufficient to detect a meaningful disparity, a bar that many single-employer deployments will not clear without pooling data across a longer window.[21]

evidence.gloss: Category exclusion rule under 2% threshold
evidence.verbatim: A category may be excluded from the audit only if it represents less than 2% of the audit data, and any such exclusion must be published along with its justification and the excluded category's applicant count and rate.[24]

evidence.gloss: Multi-category (non-binary) rankings don't map cleanly to formulas
evidence.verbatim: A model that classifies candidates into more than two categories, without emitting an underlying numerical score, does not map cleanly onto either the selection-rate or scoring-rate formula — auditors must decide whether to retain the granular categories, collapse them into a binary classification, or otherwise transform the output, and the appropriate choice depends on how the ranking is actually used downstream.[26]

evidence.gloss: Small-sample groups must be disclosed and explained, not silently dropped
evidence.verbatim: Where a demographic group has too few data points for statistical reliability, the audit must explain why that group was excluded and disclose how many candidates fell into the unknown or excluded category[14].

evidence.gloss: Local Law 144 requires intersectional testing beyond standard EEOC practice
evidence.verbatim: Local Law 144 requires testing of intersectional categories combining sex and race/ethnicity (e.g., Black women vs. white men)[7][21], going further than standard EEOC practice, which typically compares only single categories like men vs. women or one racial group vs. another[19].

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule wasn't designed for intersectional testing
evidence.verbatim: But the four-fifths rule was not designed for this.

evidence.gloss: Kim: passing single-category tests can mask intersectional bias
evidence.verbatim: Kim notes that a tool "could have something that satisfied the four-fifths rule [for] men versus women, Blacks versus whites, but it might disguise a bias against Black women"[20] — meaning the standard headline test can pass while masking a real intersectional disparity.

evidence.gloss: Sample size undermines intersectional testing even when performed
evidence.verbatim: Even where intersectional testing is performed, sample size undermines it.

evidence.gloss: Auditors find intersectional slices too small to be statistically meaningful
evidence.verbatim: Auditors have found "intersectional slices for minority categories for which the amount of data in each category is so limited that the results are misleading, in that they do not represent statistically significant segments"[17].

evidence.gloss: Auditor's dilemma: releasing low-sample numbers may falsely imply discrimination
evidence.verbatim: This creates what one auditor calls a genuine dilemma: "releasing the numbers for these categories may imply discrimination when the evidence of discrimination is simply not there"[17].

evidence.gloss: DCWP allows excluding categories under 2% of dataset, with justification and reporting
evidence.verbatim: DCWP's rules allow an independent auditor to exclude any category representing less than 2% of the audit dataset, provided the auditor documents a justification and still reports the excluded category's applicant count and rate[22][3].

h3.h3: Missing and unclassifiable demographic data

evidence.gloss: Voluntary demographic disclosure skews completeness toward advanced candidates
evidence.verbatim: Because race/ethnicity and sex disclosure is typically voluntary and collected at varying points in the pipeline, organizations tend to have more complete demographic data on candidates who advance to interview or hire.

evidence.gloss: Missing demographic data concentrates among rejected candidates
evidence.verbatim: If a tool's output correlates with who advances, this produces a disproportionate share of missing demographic data among lower-scored or rejected candidates — precisely the population the audit most needs to test.[26]

evidence.gloss: No imputing/inferring demographic data when using Historical Data
evidence.verbatim: Where Historical Data is used, employers and employment agencies may not impute or infer candidates' demographic information[37].

evidence.gloss: GDPR-driven data minimization leaves vendors without protected-attribute data
evidence.verbatim: Because many vendors intentionally limit collection of demographic data to comply with data-minimization requirements under laws like GDPR, they often lack the protected-attribute data (race, gender) needed to run the required tests in the first place[36].

evidence.gloss: Low candidate self-report rates, paralleling fair-lending compliance
evidence.verbatim: Candidates are frequently reluctant to self-report this data post-hoc — a pattern also documented in financial services, which sees very low survey response rates when collecting demographic data after the fact for fair-lending compliance[36].

evidence.gloss: Synthetic/representative data used as workaround, but science is limited
evidence.verbatim: In the absence of self-reported data, vendors sometimes turn to synthetic data or globally representative datasets, but the underlying science here is described as "fairly limited," creating uncertainty that "could cause some audits to under or overestimate bias"[36].

evidence.gloss: Ground-truth proxies like hiring outcomes can carry their own bias
evidence.verbatim: A further complication: proxies for "ground truth" such as whether a candidate was hired or advanced are themselves human judgments and may carry their own discriminatory signal[36].

evidence.gloss: imputed/inferred demographic data cannot substitute for required audit data
evidence.verbatim: Demographic classification also has a hard rule: imputed or inferred demographic data may not substitute for the required data in the audit[1].

evidence.gloss: Audit cannot test what it cannot classify
evidence.verbatim: The audit cannot test what it cannot classify.

evidence.gloss: Imputed data can't substitute; unknowns must be reported separately, not dropped
evidence.verbatim: Where a candidate's race or gender cannot be determined from available data, "DCWP says imputed or inferred demographic data may not replace the required data"[1][6] — the auditor must report the count of "unknown" individuals separately rather than silently dropping them, since silent exclusion "tends to understate adverse impact for smaller groups"[8].

evidence.gloss: Missing demographic data skews toward lower-scoring rows, a structural blind spot
evidence.verbatim: Missing demographic data is not evenly distributed either: lower-scoring or unsuccessful-classification rows tend to have more missing demographic values, meaning "a disproportionately large portion of records with lower scores or unsuccessful classifications cannot be used for testing during the audit process" — a structural blind spot in exactly the outcomes the audit is meant to scrutinize[19].

sections_menu.h2: The bias-audit math: selection rate, impact ratio, and the four-fifths rule

h3.h3: What the four-fifths rule is and where it comes from

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule as federal adverse-impact benchmark
evidence.verbatim: The four-fifths rule (also called the 80% rule) is the federal benchmark for adverse impact, applied to AI-driven hiring tools the same as to any other selection procedure[5].

evidence.gloss: Exact regulatory wording of the four-fifths rule
evidence.verbatim: The rule: "the agencies will generally consider a selection rate for any race, sex, or ethnic group which is less than four-fifths (4/5ths) or eighty percent (80%) of the selection rate for the group with the highest selection rate as a substantially different rate of selection"[5].

evidence.gloss: Ratio threshold that triggers investigation
evidence.verbatim: Ratios under 0.80 warrant investigation[6].

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule flags a ratio under 80% as adverse impact evidence
evidence.verbatim: The four-fifths rule, drawn from EEOC Guidelines, generally treats a ratio under 80% as evidence of adverse impact, though the auditor may also apply statistical significance tests.[20]

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule as informal adverse-impact threshold
evidence.verbatim: Local Law 144 does not explicitly endorse a pass/fail threshold, but the scoring-rate impact ratio is structurally similar to the EEOC's four-fifths rule: if one group's selection or scoring rate falls below 80% (0.80) of the rate for the highest-scoring group, the result is treated as evidence of possible adverse impact warranting investigation.[24][17][20][25][23]

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule's limitations and no minimum sample size guidance
evidence.verbatim: This threshold is imperfect — it can produce discrepant results against other statistical measures and generate false positives with small sample sizes — and Local Law 144 provides no explicit guidance on minimum sample size, though its delayed enforcement timeline was intended to give employers more time to accumulate data.[23]

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule: an impact ratio under 0.80 signals a violation warranting investigation
evidence.verbatim: The four-fifths rule treats a ratio under 0.80 as a signal warranting investigation

evidence.gloss: Once classified as an AEDT, chatbot screeners follow the same bias-audit math as any AEDT category
evidence.verbatim: Once a chatbot screener is classified as an AEDT, the same bias-audit math applies to it as to any other AEDT category

evidence.gloss: The four-fifths rule threshold for adverse impact
evidence.verbatim: The commonly applied screening threshold is the four-fifths rule: an impact ratio below 0.80 (80%) is treated as an initial indicator of adverse impact[19][32][33].

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule defines the core disparate impact test
evidence.verbatim: The core technical test is disparate impact analysis using the four-fifths rule from the EEOC's 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures: a selection rate for any race, sex, or ethnic group below four-fifths (80%) of the rate for the highest-selected group is generally regarded as evidence of adverse impact[4][38].

evidence.gloss: Four-fifths rule as the primary quantitative adverse-impact test, codified in UGESP 1978
evidence.verbatim: The four-fifths rule is the primary quantitative test for adverse impact used by federal enforcement agencies, codified in the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (UGESP) in 1978: "a selection rate for any race, sex, or ethnic group which is less than four-fifths (4/5) (or eighty percent) of the rate for the group with the highest rate will generally be regarded by the Federal enforcement agencies as evidence of adverse impact," while a rate above that threshold "will generally not be regarded" as evidence of adverse impact[10][11].

evidence.gloss: The rule measures outcomes, not intent, and applies to any selection method
evidence.verbatim: The rule is an outcome measure, not a motive measure — no discriminatory intent is required, and any test, screening rubric, interview format, or algorithm can produce a disparity that trips it[12].

evidence.gloss: Explains the EEOC four-fifths adverse-impact rule and why funnel audits catch violations early
evidence.verbatim:
Adverse impact is not a theory. Under the EEOC’s four-fifths rule, if one group’s selection rate falls below 80% of the highest-scoring group’s rate at any stage, regulators treat that as evidence worth investigating, whether or not anyone intended to discriminate.
This is the same threshold we flagged in our breakdown of adverse impact in cognitive ability testing, and it applies to any stage of your funnel, not just testing. A funnel audit is what catches a four-fifths violation before a regulator or a plaintiff’s attorney does.

h3.h3: How the impact ratio is calculated, step by step

evidence.gloss: Audit's core calculation is disparate impact via impact ratio across demographic categories
evidence.verbatim: The audit's core calculation is disparate impact: selection rates are compared across demographic categories (sex, including male, female, and non-binary/other; race/ethnicity across EEOC categories; and intersectional categories such as sex crossed with race/ethnicity, for example comparing outcomes for Black women against white men) and expressed as an impact ratio, the rate for a given group divided by the rate for the highest-selected group.[17][19]

evidence.gloss: Continuous-score outputs need a different audit method
evidence.verbatim: Where a matching tool produces a continuous rather than binary output — a fit score rather than a simple pass/reject — the audit methodology differs from a straightforward selection-rate calculation.

evidence.gloss: NYC LL144 scoring rate defined via median split
evidence.verbatim: Under NYC Local Law 144, an AEDT that scores candidates is tested using a **scoring rate**: the scores are binarized against the sample's median score, so that candidates scoring above the median fall into a "pass" bucket and those below fall into "fail."[20][23]

evidence.gloss: Scoring rate feeds into impact ratio
evidence.verbatim: The scoring rate for each subgroup is then used to calculate an **impact ratio** in the same way as a selection rate — a given group's rate divided by the rate of the most-favored group.[20][23]

evidence.gloss: Table: selection rate definition
evidence.verbatim: Selection rate | The proportion of each demographic group selected or advanced by the AEDT[20]

evidence.gloss: Table: scoring rate definition
evidence.verbatim: Scoring rate | For scoring AEDTs, the proportion of each group receiving a score above the sample median[20]

evidence.gloss: Table: impact ratio definition
evidence.verbatim: Impact ratio | The selection rate (or scoring rate) of a given group divided by the rate of the most-favored group[20]

evidence.gloss: LL144 bias audit method: selection/scoring rate per demographic group and an impact ratio, across sex, race/ethnicity, and intersections
evidence.verbatim: Under Local Law 144, the required independent bias audit calculates a selection rate (or scoring rate) for each demographic category and an impact ratio — each group's rate divided by the highest-scoring group's rate — across sex (including non-binary), race/ethnicity per EEOC categories, and sex-by-race/ethnicity intersections[19].

evidence.gloss: Bias-audit methodology: selection rate, impact ratio, and the demographic categories covered
evidence.verbatim: calculate the selection rate (or scoring rate) for each demographic category, then compute the impact ratio — the ratio between each group's rate and the group with the highest rate — across sex (including male, female, and non-binary/other), race/ethnicity (all EEOC categories), and intersectional categories (sex crossed with race/ethnicity)[19].

evidence.gloss: Calculation step 1: compute each group's selection rate
evidence.verbatim: Calculate the selection rate for each group being compared (number selected ÷ number who applied), typically broken out by race, ethnicity, and sex.

evidence.gloss: Calculation step 2: identify the benchmark/reference group
evidence.verbatim: Identify the highest selection rate among the groups — this becomes the benchmark or "reference group.

evidence.gloss: Calculation step 3: compute each group's impact ratio against the benchmark
evidence.verbatim: Calculate the impact ratio for every other group by dividing that group's selection rate by the benchmark rate.

evidence.gloss: Calculation step 4: compare each ratio to the 0.80 threshold
evidence.verbatim: Compare each ratio to 0.80. Any group whose ratio falls below 0.80 may signal adverse impact.

evidence.gloss: Impact ratio must be computed separately per cohort, not blended
evidence.verbatim: A key operational rule: the impact ratio must be computed separately for every cohort — a single hiring round can clear the threshold on gender while failing on race, and vice versa[12].

h3.h3: Worked examples of the calculation

evidence.gloss: Worked example of the four-fifths calculation
evidence.verbatim: Worked example: a trucking company hires 20 of 300 male applicants (6.6%) and 10 of 180 female applicants (5.5%). Dividing 5.5% by 6.6% yields 0.833 (83.3%), which clears the 80% threshold and shows no adverse impact[5].

evidence.gloss: Worked example of impact ratio calculation (0.67)
evidence.verbatim: A worked example: if men are selected at 60% and women at 40%, the impact ratio for women is 40/60, or 0.67.[19]

evidence.gloss: Worked example of the four-fifths rule: 60% men vs 40% women selected gives a 0.67 impact ratio
evidence.verbatim: for example, if men are selected at 60% and women at 40%, the impact ratio for women is 40/60 = 0.67[19]

evidence.gloss: Worked numeric example of the four-fifths calculation
evidence.verbatim: A worked example: in a pool of 135 applicants (72 non-minority, 63 minority) sitting the same screen, if 7 non-minority and 3 minority candidates are hired, the selection rates are 9.7% and 4.8% respectively, producing an impact ratio of 4.8 ÷ 9.7 = 49.5% — below the 80% threshold, indicating adverse impact[38].

evidence.gloss: Worked example setup: 135-applicant pool split by minority status
evidence.verbatim: From a talent pool of 135 applicants (72 non-minority, 63 minority) sitting the same written test[12][10]:

evidence.gloss: Worked example table: non-minority vs. minority selection and impact rates
evidence.verbatim:
| Group | Applicants | Hires | Selection rate | Impact ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Non-minority | 72 | 7 | 9.7% | 1.
| Minority | 63 | 3 | 4.8% | 0.49–0.

evidence.gloss: Race example conclusion: ratio well below 0.80 indicates adverse impact
evidence.verbatim: Because 0.49–0.495 is well below 0.80, this result indicates adverse impact against minority applicants[12][10].

evidence.gloss: Same pool re-analyzed by sex gives a different result
evidence.verbatim: The same pool viewed by sex produces a different outcome[12][10]:

evidence.gloss: Worked example table: female vs. male selection and impact rates
evidence.verbatim:
| Group | Applicants | Hires | Selection rate | Impact ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Female | 51 | 4 | 7.8% | 1.
| Male | 84 | 6 | 7.1% | 0.

evidence.gloss: Sex example conclusion: ratio clears 0.80 despite race failing
evidence.verbatim: At 0.91, this clears the 0.80 threshold and shows no adverse impact on gender, even though the same applicant pool failed the test on race/minority status[12][10].

evidence.gloss: Second worked example: white vs. Black applicant hiring counts
evidence.verbatim: A second example: out of 100 white applicants, 50 are hired (50% selection rate); out of 50 Black applicants, 15 are hired (30% selection rate).

evidence.gloss: Second example's ratio calculation shows potential adverse impact
evidence.verbatim: The ratio is 30% ÷ 50% = 60%, below 80%, suggesting potential adverse impact against Black applicants[13].

evidence.gloss: Explains how to detect a biased test using the four-fifths rule, with a worked 60%-vs-40% pass-rate example and follow-up validation questions.
evidence.verbatim:
You measure it. The first check is the four-fifths rule: compare the pass rate of each group to the group with the highest pass rate. If any group clears the test at less than 80% of that top rate, you likely have adverse impact worth investigating. It is a starting signal, not a verdict, but it tells you exactly where to look.
Say your highest-passing group clears a coding test at 60%, and another group clears it at 40%. That second rate is 67% of the first, under the 80% threshold, so the test warrants a closer look. From there you check two things: is every question tied to the job, and does the score actually predict on-the-job performance? A test that passes both can still show a gap for reasons outside the test, but a validated, job-relevant assessment gives you a defensible answer when someone asks why the numbers look the way they do. This is also where a clear record of objective hiring assessments pays off, because you can show your work.

h3.h3: Intersectional categories and unknown-demographic counts

evidence.gloss: Intersectional analysis catches compounded disparities group metrics miss
evidence.verbatim: Beyond these, **intersectional analysis** examines how overlapping identities (race, gender, class, religion, sexual orientation, disability) compound disparities that group-level metrics miss — a system might show no bias when race or gender is assessed separately yet perform poorly for candidates at the intersection of both[5].

evidence.gloss: Buolamwini and Gebru facial-recognition bias research
evidence.verbatim: This concern is grounded in facial-recognition research by Buolamwini and Gebru showing gender-classification error rates near 30% for darker-skinned women, far higher than for other groups[5]

evidence.gloss: DeGraffenreid v. General Motors intersectional-claim precedent
evidence.verbatim: in DeGraffenreid v. General Motors, where courts dismissed a combined race-and-gender discrimination claim because the factors were evaluated separately rather than jointly[5].

evidence.gloss: Calculations run per sex, race/ethnicity, and intersections
evidence.verbatim: These calculations must be run separately for each sex category, each race/ethnicity category, and their intersections (for example, Hispanic or Latino male candidates).[20]

evidence.gloss: Intersectional analysis method
evidence.verbatim: Intersectional analysis examines how combined identities — race, gender, class, and other protected characteristics — can compound disparities that single-axis testing misses; a system can appear balanced on sex and balanced on race separately while still disadvantaging one specific sex-by-race subgroup.[24][5]

evidence.gloss: Unknown/not-disclosed demographic responses must be tracked, not silently dropped
evidence.verbatim: "Unknown / not disclosed" demographic responses must be tracked explicitly rather than dropped silently from the audit[32].

evidence.gloss: Ratio must be computed per cohort and intersectional category
evidence.verbatim: Critically, the ratio must be calculated separately for every cohort and every intersectional category (e.g., comparing Black women against white men) — a tool can clear the threshold on gender while failing on race in the same hiring round[17][38].

evidence.gloss: Rules on publishing unknown-demographic counts and small-category exclusion
evidence.verbatim: The final NYC rules require the audit to additionally publish the number of individuals whose race and gender are "unknown" and thus excluded from the calculations, and permit an auditor to exclude any category representing less than 2% of the audit data, provided the summary states the justification along with that category's applicant count and rate[34][2].

evidence.gloss: unclassifiable individuals must be reported as a separate unknown-count, not excluded
evidence.verbatim: Where individuals cannot be classified into a demographic category from available data, the auditor must report the count of unknown-category individuals separately rather than silently excluding them, since exclusion tends to understate adverse impact for smaller groups[8].

h3.h3: Audit techniques beyond adverse-impact analysis

evidence.gloss: Three standard bias-audit toolkit techniques (intro)
evidence.verbatim: Three techniques are described as standard components of a bias-audit toolkit[6]:

evidence.gloss: Adverse Impact Analysis technique defined
evidence.verbatim: **Adverse Impact Analysis (Four-Fifths Rule):** compute selection rates per group and compare to the highest-scoring group; ratios under 0.80 flag investigation[6].

evidence.gloss: Structured Bias Audits technique defined
evidence.verbatim: **Structured Bias Audits:** methodologies modeled on NYC's mandate, requiring impact ratios and documentation of features, oversight, and results[6].

evidence.gloss: Counterfactual Tests technique defined
evidence.verbatim: **Counterfactual Tests:** "what-if" experiments that swap names, standardize formatting, or alter accents while holding qualifications constant; a swing in results indicates embedded bias[6].

evidence.gloss: Bias-reduction methods paired with detection techniques
evidence.verbatim: Bias-reduction methods paired with these detection techniques include adversarial debiasing, explainability tools such as SHAP and LIME, human oversight, and blind hiring[5].

h3.h3: Monitoring adverse impact across the hiring funnel, every cycle

evidence.gloss: Best practice 7: monitor adverse impact each hiring cycle using the four-fifths rule as an ongoing habit, not a one-off audit.
evidence.verbatim: A test can look fair and still produce uneven results, so measure the outcomes. After each cycle, compare pass rates across groups using the four-fifths rule (more on that below). If a gap appears, that is not automatic proof of discrimination, but it is a clear prompt to review the test items and scoring. Bias monitoring is not a one-time audit. It is a standing habit, because roles, candidate pools, and questions all drift over time.

evidence.gloss: Best practice 9: pilot and revalidate tests regularly since fairness drifts over time; includes a table mapping each bias type to its mitigating practice.
evidence.verbatim:
Run a new test on a sample that looks like your real candidate pool before it gates anyone. Check that scores relate to performance and that pass rates hold up across groups. Then put it on a review schedule, because a test that was fair two years ago can drift as the role and the market change. Treat validation as maintenance, not a launch-day checkbox.
The table below maps the most common bias types to how they surface in a test and the practice that keeps each one in check.
Bias typeHow it shows up in a testPractice that reduces it
Content biasIdioms, cultural references, or knowledge unrelated to the roleJob analysis plus plain, inclusive language
Scoring biasOpen answers graded by feel, inconsistent across reviewersStandardized rubric and structured scoring
Algorithmic biasAI scorer trained on skewed past hiresHuman-led review and adverse-impact audits of the tool
Accessibility biasFormats that exclude candidates with disabilitiesScreen-reader support, extra time, easy accommodations
Confirmation biasResume impression bleeding into test scoresBlind scoring and multiple reviewers

evidence.gloss: Key takeaways recapping structure, job analysis, validation as legal defense, adverse-impact monitoring, human-audited AI, and fairness as ongoing maintenance.
evidence.verbatim:
- Structure beats intuition. A standardized, consistently scored test removes the space where gut-feel bias operates, and it predicts performance better too. Sackett et al. put structured methods ahead of cognitive ability, so fairness and accuracy pull in the same direction rather than against each other.
- Job analysis is the root fix. Test only what the role needs and most content bias never gets in, because there is no room for cultural trivia or pedigree signals that measure background instead of skill.
- Validation is your legal defense. If a test screens out a protected group unevenly, EEOC guidance asks you to prove it predicts performance. A validated, job-relevant assessment is the evidence that answers that question.
- Measure adverse impact every cycle. The four-fifths rule is a cheap early-warning system. A pass rate below 80% of the top group’s rate is your prompt to review items and scoring before the gap compounds.
- AI needs a human owner. Automated screening can cut or amplify bias, and the 85% name-preference finding shows how fast it goes wrong unchecked. Audit the tool and keep a person accountable for every decision.
- Fairness is maintenance, not a launch task. Roles and candidate pools drift, so pilot new tests, re-validate on a schedule, and treat monitoring as an ongoing habit rather than a one-time audit.

evidence.gloss: Measuring bias-free hiring means tracking pass-through rates by group per stage against the EEOC 80% threshold, not asking managers if it felt fair
evidence.verbatim: You measure it by tracking pass-through rates by group at every funnel stage, not by asking managers if the process felt fair. A gap that clears the EEOC’s 80% threshold at any single stage is your signal to dig into that stage specifically.

evidence.gloss: Table of metrics and red flags to track at each funnel stage (applied, screened, interviewed, offered, hired), run quarterly
evidence.verbatim:
Funnel stageWhat to trackRed flag
AppliedSource and demographic mix of applicantsOne channel drives 80%+ of applicants
ScreenedPass rate by group vs. the highest-scoring groupBelow 80% of the top group’s rate (four-fifths rule)
InterviewedInterview-to-offer rate by group and by interviewerLarge spread between interviewers scoring the same rubric
OfferedOffer acceptance rate and starting comp by groupConsistent comp gap at the same level
Hired90-day performance and retention by source and groupRetention gap tied to hiring channel, not role
Run this audit quarterly. A single bad quarter is noise; the same stage failing two quarters running is a process problem.

sections_menu.h2: The independent bias audit: who runs it, what it costs, how often

h3.h3: Who counts as an independent auditor under Local Law 144

evidence.gloss: Local Law 144 definition of Independent Auditor
evidence.verbatim: The audit must be conducted by an "Independent Auditor" — defined under NYC Local Law 144's final rules as an objective individual or group that is not and has not been involved in the use, development, or distribution of the AEDT; has not at any point been employed by the employer, vendor, or developer; and has no direct or material indirect financial interest in the tool or the vendor[34].

evidence.gloss: Independence is a legal requirement aligned with EEOC guidelines
evidence.verbatim: This is not merely a best practice — Local Law 144 explicitly requires independence, and it aligns with broader EEOC expectations under the 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures[4].

evidence.gloss: Research supports higher quality of independent third-party audits
evidence.verbatim: Prior research found that audits conducted by an independent third party tend to be of higher quality than those conducted by an internal team or a contracted second-party assessor (Bennett et al., 2013; Deis Jr and Giroux, 1992; Tepalagul and Lin, 2015)[35].

evidence.gloss: Vendors may self-audit if the auditing team differs from the build team

AI can help by stripping names, photos, and demographics out of screening. It can also make bias worse at scale when it learns from a skewed history. A 2024 University of Washington study found three language models favored white-associated names 85% of the time when ranking otherwise identical resumes. So use AI to organize and surface evidence, audit any AI scorer for adverse impact the same way you would a human panel, and keep a person accountable for the call. Automation that no one checks is not neutral. It just repeats yesterday’s bias faster.
Pro Tip: Before you trust any AI screening tool, ask the vendor for its adverse-impact results by group, and run your own check after 30 to 50 candidates. If they cannot show you the numbers, treat the tool as unvalidated and keep a human reviewer on every decision.

The practical stance is simple. Let AI assist (organize evidence, flag inconsistencies, summarize skills) and keep the decision human. Audit the tool for adverse impact on your own candidate data, not just the vendor’s demo. And never let an AI score be the only thing standing between a candidate and a rejection. evidence.verbatim: Every question should trace back to a skill the job analysis flagged. h3.h3: Where assessments and proctoring fit

evidence.gloss: FAQ answers on what makes an assessment legally fair, ideal assessment length, whether AI tools can be fair, and how to balance anti-cheating with privacy.
evidence.verbatim:
What makes a hiring assessment legally fair?
A hiring assessment is legally fair when it tests skills directly tied to the job, applies the same conditions to every candidate, and shows no adverse impact across protected demographic groups. The EEOC, EU AI Act, and most national labor laws use these three tests.
Documentation matters as much as design. Companies must keep records of test validation, scoring criteria, and demographic outcome reviews.
How long should a fair hiring assessment take?
Most fair assessments take 30 to 60 minutes for early-stage screening. Longer assessments fatigue candidates and introduce variance that has nothing to do with skill.
Senior or specialist roles can use longer project-based simulations of two to four hours. Pay candidates for any assessment that exceeds two hours of focused work.
Can AI hiring tools be fair?
AI hiring tools can be fair when they use validated training data, undergo regular bias audits, and operate under human oversight. Tools that train on historical hiring data without correction often replicate past bias.
How do you prevent cheating without invading candidate privacy?
Use proportionate proctoring that matches the stakes of the role. Browser lockdown and tab tracking suit most early-stage tests. Webcam and screen recording suit senior or technical roles where skill verification matters most.
Disclose every monitoring feature in advance. Candidates who know what gets tracked rarely complain about fair monitoring.
How often should you update your hiring assessments?
Refresh assessments at least once a year and any time the job description changes meaningfully. Question banks leak online over time, and job demands evolve faster than most companies expect.
Quarterly bias audits catch drift between full refreshes. Set the cadence on your hiring calendar and stick to it.
